explanation: Draw an equilateral triangle to create a 60° angle since all interior angles are 60°.
name: Constructing a 60° Angle Using an Equilateral Triangle

explanation: Join the point to the circle’s centre; draw the line perpendicular to this radius at the point to get the tangent.
name: Constructing a Tangent to a Circle at a Given Point

explanation: Draw a side and the included angle with the adjacent side length; construct a line parallel to the base through the far vertex and transfer the opposite side length.
name: Constructing a Parallelogram from Two Sides and Included Angle

explanation: With a compass, draw arcs from each endpoint with equal radius crossing above and below the segment; join the intersections.
name: Constructing the Perpendicular Bisector of a Segment

explanation: From the angle’s vertex, draw an arc intersecting both rays; from these intersections draw arcs that cross; join the vertex to the crossing point.
name: Constructing the Angle Bisector

explanation: Construct two perpendicular bisectors of sides to locate the circumcentre; draw the circle with radius to a vertex.
name: Constructing the Circumcircle of a Triangle

explanation: Construct two angle bisectors to locate the incentre; drop a perpendicular to a side for the radius; draw the circle tangent to all sides.
name: Constructing the Incircle of a Triangle

explanation: Find midpoints of two sides, draw medians from opposite vertices; their intersection is the centroid.
name: Constructing the Centroid of a Triangle

explanation: Draw two altitudes by constructing lines through vertices perpendicular to the opposite sides; their intersection is the orthocentre.
name: Constructing the Orthocentre of a Triangle

explanation: The circumcircle passes through all three vertices; its centre (circumcentre) is where perpendicular bisectors meet.
name: Circumcircle and Circumcentre of a Triangle

explanation: The incircle is tangent to all three sides; its centre (incentre) is where angle bisectors meet.
name: Incircle and Incentre of a Triangle

explanation: A segment joining a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side; the three medians concur at the centroid.
name: Median of a Triangle

explanation: A perpendicular from a vertex to the opposite side (or its extension); the three altitudes concur at the orthocentre.
name: Altitude of a Triangle

explanation: Any point on the perpendicular bisector of a segment is equidistant from the segment’s endpoints.
name: Perpendicular Bisector Locus Theorem

explanation: Any point on the bisector of an angle is equidistant from the angle’s sides.
name: Angle Bisector Locus Theorem

explanation: Intersect two perpendicular bisectors of sides of the triangle formed by the points to locate the common equidistant point.
name: Finding a Point Equidistant from Three Points

explanation: The circumcentre lies at the midpoint of the hypotenuse in a right-angled triangle.
name: Circumcentre in Right-Angled Triangles

explanation: The circumcentre of an obtuse triangle lies outside the triangle.
name: Circumcentre in Obtuse Triangles

explanation: Interpreting ratio scales (e.g., 1:n) to convert lengths and using k^2 to convert areas between plan/model and reality.
name: Working with Map and Model Scales

explanation: Finding a function F whose derivative is a given function f; written as ∫ f(x) dx = F(x) + c.
name: Antiderivative (Indefinite Integral)

explanation: Integrate x^n by increasing the power by 1 and dividing by the new power: ∫ x^n dx = x^{n+1}/(n+1) + c for n ≠ -1.
name: Power Rule for Integration

explanation: Constants factor out and sums integrate termwise: ∫(af + bg) dx = a∫f dx + b∫g dx.
name: Linearity of the Integral

explanation: The arbitrary constant c in indefinite integrals, determined by an initial condition or point on the curve.
name: Constant of Integration

broader_concept: Definite Integrals and Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
explanation: Use an antiderivative F to compute ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a); the +c cancels.
name: Evaluating Definite Integrals via Antiderivatives (FTC)

explanation: Area between y = f(x) and the x-axis from x = a to x = b is A = ∫_a^b f(x) dx.
name: Area Under a Curve Using Definite Integrals

explanation: If curves intersect at x = a and x = b, the area is ∫_a^b [g(x) − f(x)] dx where g is above f.
name: Area Between Two Curves

explanation: Integrals above the x-axis are positive and below are negative; geometric area uses absolute values per region.
name: Sign of Definite Integral and Absolute Area

explanation: When area is bounded by a curve and the y-axis, write x = f(y) and use A = ∫_a^b x dy.
name: Area with Respect to y (Integrating x dy)

explanation: Standard integral: ∫ e^{ax} dx = (1/a) e^{ax} + c for constant a ≠ 0.
name: Integrating Exponential Functions e^{ax}

explanation: Standard integral: ∫ a^{x} dx = a^{x}/ln(a) + c for a > 0, a ≠ 1.
name: Integrating Exponential Functions a^{x}

explanation: Standard integrals: ∫ cos(ax) dx = sin(ax)/a + c and ∫ sin(ax) dx = −cos(ax)/a + c.
name: Integrating Sine and Cosine with Linear Arguments

explanation: Integrate compositions when the derivative of the inner function is a factor: set u = g(x), du = g'(x) dx.
name: Reverse Chain Rule (u-Substitution) for Integration

explanation: A standard result: ∫ ln x dx = x ln x − x + c for x > 0.
name: Integrating ln x

explanation: Manipulate the integrand (expand, divide termwise, rewrite roots as fractional powers) to apply ∫ ax^n dx rules.
name: Rewriting Integrands Using Algebra to Enable Power Rule

explanation: Recover velocity from acceleration and displacement from velocity by integrating with respect to time; use initial conditions.
name: Kinematics via Integration

explanation: Solve equations of curves/lines to find intersection x- (or y-) values that serve as bounds for area integrals.
name: Determining Limits of Integration from Intersections

explanation: Find k so that ∫_k^b f(x) dx = ∫_a^k f(x) dx, solving for the vertical line x = k that splits area into equal parts.
name: Partitioning Area Equally to Find a Divider

explanation: Interpreting f'(x) as the instantaneous rate of change of y with respect to x and the slope of the tangent line to the curve at a point.
name: Derivative as Slope of the Tangent

explanation: Find dy/dx, evaluate at the point, then use y − y1 = m(x − x1) to obtain the tangent line.
name: Equation of a Tangent Line Using Derivatives

explanation: Setting f'(x) equal to the slope of the target line to find points where the tangent is parallel.
name: Tangents Parallel to a Given Line

explanation: Determining where a function increases (f'(x) > 0) or decreases (f'(x) < 0) by analyzing the sign of the derivative.
name: Increasing and Decreasing via First Derivative

explanation: Solving inequalities like f'(x) > 0 by factoring and using sign charts to identify intervals of increase or decrease.
name: Interval Analysis with Sign Charts for f'(x)

explanation: Showing f'(x) is always positive or negative by completing the square or other positivity arguments.
name: Proving Monotonicity for All x Using Algebraic Positivity

explanation: Finding critical points by solving f'(x)=0 and then computing corresponding y-values to locate stationary points.
name: Stationary Points from f'(x)=0

explanation: Classifying a stationary point: if f''(x0) < 0 then local maximum; if f''(x0) > 0 then local minimum.
name: Second Derivative Test for Local Extrema

explanation: Determining the nature of a stationary point by checking whether f'(x) changes sign from + to − (max) or − to + (min) around the point.
name: First Derivative Sign-Change Test

explanation: Using the sign of f''(x) to determine concavity: concave up if f''(x) > 0 and concave down if f''(x) < 0.
name: Concavity and the Second Derivative

explanation: Identifying inflection points where f''(x)=0 and changes sign, indicating a change in concavity.
name: Point of Inflection via f''(x)=0 with Sign Change

explanation: A point where f'(x)=0 and the tangent is horizontal, but the point is not a local extremum because concavity changes.
name: Horizontal Point of Inflection (Saddle Point)

explanation: Zeros of f′ correspond to stationary points of f; the sign of f′ indicates where f is increasing or decreasing.
name: Graphical Relationship Between f and f′

explanation: Creating a qualitative graph of the derivative by reading slopes: positive/negative regions and where slope is zero.
name: Sketching f′ from a Graph of f

explanation: Viewing f′(x) as a function with its own graph, representing the slope of f at each x.
name: Slope Function (Derived Function) Interpretation

explanation: Modeling a quantity in one variable, differentiating, finding critical points, and using the second derivative to determine maxima or minima.
name: Optimization with Calculus

explanation: Expressing area or volume in one variable using given constraints (e.g., fixed perimeter or volume) and optimizing via derivatives.
name: Optimization Under Geometric Constraints

explanation: Determining feasible intervals for variables from geometric or contextual conditions before optimizing.
name: Selecting Domain Constraints in Optimization

explanation: For motion in a straight line, v=ds/dt and a=dv/dt=d²s/dt²; interpreting positive, negative, and zero velocities.
name: Kinematics: Velocity and Acceleration from Displacement

explanation: Solving v(t)=0 to determine times when a particle is momentarily at rest; then evaluating acceleration if needed.
name: Finding Instantaneous Rest in Kinematics

explanation: Using dy/dt = (dy/du)(du/dt) to link given and required rates when variables depend on time.
name: Related Rates via the Chain Rule

explanation: Recognizing that dt/dr = 1/(dr/dt) when both rates are defined and nonzero.
name: Reciprocal Relationships Between Rates

explanation: Computing dA/dt from A=πr² using dA/dt = 2πr·dr/dt to find how the circle’s area changes over time.
name: Related Rates in Circular Geometry

explanation: Using V as a function of depth h to derive dh/dt from a given dV/dt via the chain rule.
name: Related Rates for Volume–Depth Models

explanation: Applying the Pythagorean relationship with implicit differentiation to relate dx/dt and dy/dt for sliding ladders.
name: Related Rates in Right Triangles (Ladder Problem)

explanation: Establishing that a rational function is increasing or decreasing everywhere by showing f'(x) maintains a constant sign.
name: Monotonicity of Rational Functions via Derivative Sign

explanation: Using the linear form y − y1 = m(x − x1) with m = f'(x1) to write the tangent line at a point.
name: Point-Slope Form for Tangent Lines

explanation: Factoring polynomials and using sign analysis to solve inequalities that arise from f'(x) > 0 or f'(x) < 0.
name: Solving Polynomial Inequalities via Factorization

explanation: Computes the future value of a principal P invested at effective rate i per period for t periods.
name: Compound Interest Final Value F = P(1+i)^t

explanation: Finds the current value of a future amount F due in t periods at effective rate i using discounting.
name: Present Value by Discounting P = F/(1+i)^t

explanation: Converts an effective annual rate i (AER) to an effective periodic rate r with m compounding periods per year, and vice versa.
name: Effective Periodic Rate Conversion (1+r)^m = 1+i

explanation: Calculates the accumulated value of t equal payments P made at the beginning of each period at rate i.
name: Future Value of an Annuity Due F = P(1+i)((1+i)^t - 1)/i

explanation: Computes the cost now of t equal payments P made at the end of each period at rate i; used for pensions and loans.
name: Present Value of an Ordinary Annuity PV = P(1 - (1+i)^(-t))/i

explanation: Determines the periodic repayment A needed to amortize a loan of principal P over t periods at rate i.
name: Loan Amortization Payment A = P·i(1+i)^t/((1+i)^t - 1)

explanation: Models asset value decline by a fixed percentage i each period for t periods from initial value P.
name: Reducing Balance Depreciation F = P(1 - i)^t

explanation: Depreciates an asset by a constant amount each period, typically based on a fixed percentage of original cost.
name: Straight-Line Depreciation

explanation: Uses logarithms to find the number of periods t for a principal P to grow to F at rate i.
name: Solving for Time in Compound Growth t = ln(F/P)/ln(1+i)

explanation: Derives the annual equivalent rate i from a total return factor over n years using (1+i)^n = total factor.
name: AER from Multi-year Return via nth Root

explanation: Computes the sum of n terms of a geometric sequence; foundational for deriving annuity PV and FV formulas.
name: Sum of a Finite Geometric Series S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r)

explanation: Interprets the interest rate used to discount future cash flows to present value as the discount rate.
name: Discount Rate in Present Value Calculations

explanation: Adjusts prices or costs over time using a compound inflation rate: F = P(1+f)^t.
name: Inflation Adjustment by Compound Growth

explanation: Rearranges the amortization formula to solve for loan principal P given payment A, rate i, and periods t.
name: Calculating Maximum Loan Principal from Payment, Rate, and Term

explanation: Uses logarithmic manipulation of the amortization or annuity equations to find t given A, P, and i.
name: Solving for Number of Annuity Payments Using Logarithms

explanation: Converts ordinary annuity results to annuity-due (or vice versa) using a factor of (1+i) to account for payment timing.
name: Annuity Timing Adjustment Factor

explanation: Finding the length of an arc of a circle using l = rθ where θ is in radians.
name: Arc Length in Radians

explanation: Converting between degrees and radians using 360° = 2π radians.
name: Radian–Degree Conversion

explanation: Using the formula A = π r^2 to find the area of a circle.
name: Area of a Circle

explanation: Finding the area between two concentric sectors with the same central angle by subtracting their areas.
name: Area of an Annular Sector

explanation: Using A = base × perpendicular height to find the area of a parallelogram.
name: Area of a Parallelogram (Base × Height)

explanation: Computing area with adjacent sides x and y and included angle θ via A = xy sin θ.
name: Area of a Parallelogram Using Sine

explanation: Finding area using A = (1/2) ab sin C for two sides a, b and included angle C.
name: Triangle Area via Sine Formula

explanation: Relating sides and opposite angles in any triangle: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
name: Law of Sines

explanation: Calculating each interior angle using (n−2)×180°/n for an n-gon.
name: Interior Angle of a Regular Polygon

explanation: Using A = (1/2) × apothem × perimeter to compute area.
name: Area of a Regular Polygon via Apothem

explanation: Determining a regular polygon’s apothem from side length and central/base angles using tan or cot relations.
name: Finding the Apothem Using Trigonometry

explanation: Understanding that interior angles of a triangle sum to 180 degrees.
name: Angle Sum of a Triangle

explanation: Using fixed side ratios in 30-60-90 and 45-45-90 triangles to solve for unknown lengths.
name: Special Right Triangles (30-60-90 and 45-45-90)

explanation: Computing the diagonal length via d = √(x^2 + y^2).
name: Rectangle Diagonal Formula

explanation: Finding the diagonal of a square with side x as x√2; diagonals are perpendicular bisectors.
name: Square Diagonal Length

explanation: Understanding that diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
name: Parallelogram Diagonal Properties

explanation: A quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides.
name: Definition of a Trapezium

explanation: A quadrilateral with all vertices on a circle; opposite angles are supplementary.
name: Cyclic Quadrilateral

explanation: Any triangle inscribed in a semicircle is right-angled at the point on the circle.
name: Angle in a Semicircle (Thales' Theorem)

explanation: Calculating volume as V = (area of cross-section) × length.
name: Volume of a Prism

explanation: Unfolding a prism to a net to compute total external surface area by summing face areas.
name: Surface Area of a Prism Using Nets

explanation: Using V = πr^2h and SA = 2πr^2 + 2πrh for cylinders.
name: Cylinder Volume and Surface Area

explanation: Deriving and using A = π r ℓ for the lateral area of a cone from its sector net.
name: Curved Surface Area of a Cone

explanation: Using V = (1/3) π r^2 h to compute the volume of a cone.
name: Volume of a Cone

explanation: Using V = (4/3) π r^3 to find the volume of a sphere.
name: Volume of a Sphere

explanation: Finding the frustum volume by subtracting volumes of two similar cones after relating dimensions via similarity.
name: Volume of a Conical Frustum by Subtraction

explanation: Applying similarity ratios to relate heights and radii in solids, e.g., to determine missing frustum dimensions.
name: Using Similar Triangles in 3D Problems

explanation: Computing area under a chord as A = (1/2) r^2 (θ − sin θ) for central angle θ (radians).
name: Area of a Circular Segment

explanation: Quantifying measurement error using relative error = |estimate − true|/true and percentage error = relative error × 100%.
name: Relative and Percentage Error

explanation: Interpreting instrument precision as ± half the smallest scale division to state measurement intervals.
name: Tolerance of Measurements

explanation: Translating rounded values (e.g., to 1 decimal place) into minimum and maximum possible true values.
name: Intervals from Stated Degrees of Accuracy

explanation: Checking whether a formula’s units match an intended quantity (length, area, volume).
name: Dimensional Analysis for Formula Consistency

explanation: Calculating rectangle perimeter using P = 2(x + y).
name: Rectangle Perimeter Formula

explanation: Optimizing A in terms of r given fixed sector perimeter using completing the square and calculus-free reasoning.
name: Maximizing Sector Area with Fixed Perimeter

explanation: Interpreting area under a speed–time graph as distance traveled; estimating using trapezoidal rule.
name: Distance as Area Under a Speed–Time Graph

explanation: Represent multi-step experiments with branches labeled by probabilities when outcomes of successive trials do not affect each other.
name: Tree Diagrams for Independent Sequential Events

explanation: Use branching diagrams with updated probabilities after each draw when sampling without replacement.
name: Tree Diagrams for Dependent Events (Without Replacement)

explanation: Define a random variable taking discrete values and tabulate each value with its probability.
name: Discrete Random Variable and Probability Distribution Table

explanation: Compute the long-run average outcome by summing each value times its probability.
name: Expected Value of a Discrete Random Variable E(X)=ΣxP(x)

explanation: A game is fair if the player's expected net gain is zero.
name: Fair Game Criterion via Expected Value

explanation: Adjust the expected payout by subtracting the cost to play to evaluate profitability.
name: Net Expected Gain/Loss (Expected Value minus Cost)

explanation: As the number of trials increases, the sample mean approaches the expected value.
name: Law of Large Numbers (Average Approaches Expected Value)

explanation: A sequence with two outcomes per trial, independent trials, constant success probability, and fixed number of trials.
name: Bernoulli Trials (Conditions)

explanation: Gives the probability of exactly r successes in n independent trials with success probability p.
name: Binomial Probability Formula P(X=r)=C(n,r)p^r q^{n-r}

explanation: Probability that the first success occurs on trial n equals q^{n-1}p for independent Bernoulli trials.
name: Geometric Distribution: First Success on nth Trial

explanation: Probability that the kth success occurs on trial n equals C(n-1,k-1)p^k q^{n-k}.
name: Negative Binomial: kth Success on nth Trial

explanation: Compute probabilities like 'at least one' by 1 minus the probability of the complementary 'none' event.
name: Complement Rule for 'At Least' Events

explanation: For independent events, the probability of both occurring is the product of their probabilities.
name: Multiplication Rule for Independent Events P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B)

explanation: Defines the probability of A given B using the ratio of joint probability to the probability of B.
name: Conditional Probability Definition P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B)

explanation: Determine independence by checking whether P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).
name: Independence Test via Multiplication Rule

explanation: If events cannot occur together, P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B).
name: Addition Rule for Mutually Exclusive Events

explanation: Compute probability of A or B by adding probabilities and subtracting the overlap.
name: General Addition Rule for Unions P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A∩B)

explanation: Evaluate probabilities by counting favorable and total outcomes with combinations.
name: Combinatorial Probability Using Combinations (nCr)

explanation: Probability model for draws without replacement from finite populations categorized by type.
name: Hypergeometric Probability (Sampling Without Replacement)

explanation: Use set regions to compute probabilities of unions, intersections, and complements from counts.
name: Venn Diagrams for Probability Calculations

explanation: List all ordered pairs of results to analyze events like sums and doubles.
name: Sample Space Enumeration for Two Dice (36 Outcomes)

explanation: Calculate event probabilities when outcomes have unequal likelihoods.
name: Biased Coins and Dice: Non-uniform Probability Models

explanation: Estimate probabilities by modeling experiments with dice, spinners, or random numbers.
name: Probability Simulation (Monte Carlo) Using Random Generators

explanation: Differentiate variables that take countable values from those taking values in intervals.
name: Discrete vs Continuous Random Variables (Distinction)

explanation: Verify a probability distribution by ensuring all probabilities over outcomes add to one.
name: Sum of Probabilities Equals 1 (Distribution Validity Check)

explanation: A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain.
name: Function as a Relation with Unique Outputs

explanation: Identifying the input set (domain), the target set (codomain), and the actual outputs (range) of a function and noting that range is a subset of the codomain.
name: Domain, Codomain, and Range

explanation: A graphical test: a relation is a function if no vertical line intersects its graph more than once.
name: Vertical Line Test

explanation: Using f(x)=..., f: x -> ..., and y=... to represent functions and specifying f: A -> B to indicate domain and codomain.
name: Function Notation and Mapping Notation

explanation: Determining whether a mapping is a function by ensuring each domain element maps to exactly one codomain element.
name: Function Identification from Mapping Diagrams

explanation: Substituting numerical values or algebraic expressions into a function rule to compute outputs.
name: Evaluating Functions at Numbers and Expressions

explanation: Writing sets like {x in R | a <= x <= b} as [a,b], (a,b), [a,b), or (a,b].
name: Interval Notation for Domains and Ranges

explanation: Limiting the input set so a relation (e.g., sqrt or log) becomes a function with real outputs over the chosen domain.
name: Restricting Domains to Define Functions

explanation: Forming a composite function by using the output of one function as the input of another: (g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)).
name: Composition of Functions (g∘f)

explanation: Understanding that in general g∘f ≠ f∘g, and order matters in composition.
name: Non-Commutativity of Composition

explanation: Using f^2(x)=f(f(x)) and extending to n-fold composition.
name: Repeated Composition Notation f^n(x)

explanation: A function where distinct inputs map to distinct outputs; each output has a unique preimage.
name: Injective (One-to-One) Function

explanation: A function is injective on a domain if every horizontal line intersects its graph at most once.
name: Horizontal Line Test for Injectivity

explanation: A function whose range equals its codomain; every codomain element is an image of some domain element.
name: Surjective (Onto) Function

explanation: Choosing appropriate domain or codomain restrictions to make a function injective or surjective.
name: Achieving Injectivity or Surjectivity via Restrictions

explanation: The inverse function f^{-1} swaps inputs and outputs of f and corresponds graphically to reflection in the line y=x.
name: Inverse Function as Reverse Mapping

explanation: Replace f(x) with y, solve for x in terms of y, then interchange x and y to obtain f^{-1}(x).
name: Finding an Inverse Function Algebraically

explanation: Checking that f(f^{-1}(x))=x and f^{-1}(f(x))=x to confirm inverse relationships.
name: Verifying Inverses via Composition Equals Identity

explanation: A function has an inverse on its domain precisely when it is both injective and surjective (bijective).
name: Inverse Exists If and Only If Function Is Bijective

explanation: Rewriting ax^2+bx+c as a(x-h)^2+k to identify the vertex (h,k) and minimum/maximum value.
name: Completing the Square to Find Quadratic Vertex

explanation: Finding where a line crosses the axes by setting x=0 for the y-intercept and y=0 for the x-intercept.
name: Axis Intercepts Method for Linear Graphs

explanation: Solving the equation f(x)=0 to determine points where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis.
name: Finding x-Intercepts by Solving f(x)=0

explanation: Using factorization to locate roots, the sign of the leading coefficient for end behavior, and plotting intercepts to sketch the cubic.
name: Sketching Cubic Functions from Factors and Leading Coefficient

explanation: A repeated factor (x-a)^2 implies the graph touches but does not cross the x-axis at x=a.
name: Double Root Indicates Tangency

explanation: Setting f′(x)=0 to find points where the slope is zero (local maxima, minima, or horizontal inflection points).
name: Finding Stationary Points Using the First Derivative

explanation: Using f′′(x)>0 for local minima, f′′(x)<0 for local maxima to classify stationary points.
name: Second Derivative Test for Stationary Points

explanation: Locating where the concavity changes, often by analyzing where f′′(x)=0 and the sign of f′′(x) changes.
name: Point of Inflection Identification

explanation: Forming y=k(x−r1)(x−r2)... and using a known point on the graph to determine the leading constant k.
name: Constructing a Polynomial from Zeros and a Point

explanation: Modeling populations or quantities with continuous growth/decay; solving for parameters and time using logarithms.
name: Exponential Growth and Decay Model N=N0 e^{rt}

explanation: The function y=log_a x is the inverse of y=a^x; for natural base, y=ln x is inverse of y=e^x.
name: Logarithmic Functions as Inverses of Exponentials

explanation: Exponential y=a^x has horizontal asymptote y=0; logarithmic y=log_a x has vertical asymptote x=0.
name: Asymptotes of Exponential and Logarithmic Graphs

explanation: Shifting graphs via y=f(x)+a (vertical) and y=f(x±a) (horizontal, with opposite sign direction for x-shifts).
name: Graph Transformations: Vertical and Horizontal Translations

explanation: Reflecting via y=−f(x) (in x-axis) and y=f(−x) (in y-axis); stretching via y=a f(x) vertically by factor a.
name: Graph Transformations: Reflections and Vertical Scaling

explanation: Recognizing natural numbers, integers, rationals, irrationals, reals, and positive reals for specifying domains and ranges.
name: Standard Number Sets (N, Z, Q, R, R+)

explanation: Ensuring radicands are nonnegative (e.g., 4−x^2 ≥ 0) and log arguments are positive (x>0) when defining domains.
name: Domain Restrictions for Radical and Logarithmic Functions

explanation: From completed square y=a(x−h)^2+k, the axis of symmetry is x=h.
name: Axis of Symmetry of a Quadratic

explanation: A numerical measure of the strength and direction of linear association between two quantitative variables, taking values from -1 to 1.
name: Pearson Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient (r)

explanation: Determining the direction (positive, negative, none) and strength (weak to strong) of a linear relationship by examining the pattern of points.
name: Interpreting Correlation from Scatter Plots

explanation: Drawing a line through a scatter plot so that points are roughly balanced above and below, capturing the overall linear trend.
name: Line of Best Fit by Eye

explanation: Estimating values of one variable from another using the fitted line; interpolation is more reliable than extrapolation beyond the data range.
name: Using a Line of Best Fit for Prediction

explanation: Computing how many standard deviations a value x lies from the mean using z = (x − μ) / σ, and interpreting relative performance.
name: Standard Score (z-score) Calculation

explanation: A continuous, bell-shaped, symmetric distribution where mean = median = mode and the shape is determined by μ and σ.
name: Normal Distribution: Properties and Shape

explanation: In a normal distribution, about 68% of data lie within 1σ, 95% within 2σ, and 99.7% within 3σ of the mean.
name: Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7 Rule)

explanation: The normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1; total area under the curve is 1 and the curve is symmetric about 0.
name: Standard Normal Distribution (Z Distribution)

explanation: Looking up cumulative probabilities P(Z ≤ a) and using symmetry and complement rules to find right-tail or interval probabilities.
name: Using Z-Tables to Find Normal Probabilities

explanation: Standardizing x to z with z = (x − μ)/σ and transforming back via x = μ + zσ to compute probabilities and quantiles.
name: Converting Between X and Z for Normal Probabilities

explanation: For continuous random variables, probabilities correspond to areas under the probability density function, with total area equal to 1.
name: Probability as Area Under a Density Curve

explanation: Plotting bivariate data pairs (x, y) on Cartesian axes with appropriate scaling to visualize relationships.
name: Drawing Scatter Plots

explanation: Finding slope m = (y2 − y1)/(x2 − x1) and using y − y1 = m(x − x1) to express the line, often in the form y = A + Bx.
name: Equation of a Line from Two Points

explanation: Understanding that a strong correlation does not imply that changes in one variable cause changes in the other.
name: Correlation vs Causation

explanation: Recognizing that μ shifts the center and σ controls the spread of the normal curve, altering its location and shape.
name: Parameters of the Normal Distribution (μ and σ)

explanation: Judging the approximate magnitude and sign of r by the tightness and direction of the linear point pattern.
name: Estimating Correlation Coefficient from a Scatter Diagram

explanation: Constructing a confidence interval for a population proportion using p̂ ± 1.96·sqrt(p̂(1−p̂)/n).
name: 95% Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion (Normal Approximation)

explanation: Using E = 1/√n as a quick 95% margin of error for proportions.
name: Margin of Error Approximation for Proportions at 95% Confidence

explanation: Computing σ_{p̂} = sqrt(p(1−p)/n) and substituting p̂ when p is unknown.
name: Standard Error of a Sample Proportion

explanation: Testing H0 by checking whether the hypothesized p lies inside the 95% CI built around p̂.
name: Hypothesis Test for a Population Proportion via Confidence Interval

explanation: For large n, the sample mean is approximately normal with mean μ and standard deviation σ/√n; exactly normal if the population is normal.
name: Central Limit Theorem (Sampling Distribution of the Mean)

explanation: Standardizing a sample mean using z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n).
name: Z-Score for a Sample Mean

explanation: Constructing x̄ ± 1.96·σ/√n for the population mean when σ is known (or well-approximated for large n).
name: 95% Confidence Interval for a Population Mean with Known Sigma

explanation: Testing H0: μ = μ0 using z = (x̄ − μ0)/(σ/√n) and rejecting if |z| > 1.96 at α = 0.05.
name: Two-Tailed Z-Test for a Population Mean

explanation: Computing p = 2·P(Z > |z|) to quantify evidence against H0.
name: p-Value for a Two-Tailed Z-Test

explanation: Solving 1.96·sqrt(p(1−p)/n) = m for n to achieve margin of error m.
name: Sample Size Determination for a Proportion (Specified Margin of Error)

explanation: Solving 1.96·σ/√n = m for n to achieve a target margin of error m.
name: Sample Size Determination for a Mean (Specified Margin of Error)

explanation: Understanding that the method produces intervals that capture the true parameter in 95% of repeated samples.
name: Interpreting a 95% Confidence Interval

explanation: Computing p̂ = x/n as the proportion of successes in a sample.
name: Calculating Sample Proportion

explanation: Using p̂ ± 1/√n to give a quick 95% CI for a population proportion.
name: 95% Confidence Interval for a Proportion using Margin-of-Error Approximation

explanation: Using critical z-values ±1.96 and rejecting H0 if |z| > 1.96.
name: Critical Values and Regions for Two-Tailed Tests at 5% Significance

explanation: The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄ equals σ/√n.
name: Standard Error of the Mean

explanation: Finding probabilities such as P(a < x̄ < b) using z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) and standard normal tables.
name: Normal Probability Calculations for a Sample Mean

explanation: Recognizing that larger n decreases standard error and narrows confidence intervals.
name: Effect of Sample Size on Margin of Error

explanation: Substituting s for σ in large-sample z-based confidence intervals and tests.
name: Using Sample Standard Deviation When Population Sigma is Unknown (Large Samples)
